content: The Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region, Module 6: Neonatal Tetanus (September 2023) provides detailed guidance on the surveillance, prevention, and management of neonatal tetanus (NT). 1. Definition and Context: Neonatal tetanus (NT) is a severe disease affecting newborns, typically caused by unhygienic delivery practices or inadequate maternal immunization. It is characterized by muscle stiffness, spasms, and feeding difficulties. Maternal tetanus, defined as tetanus during pregnancy or within six weeks postpartum, shares similar risk factors and prevention strategies with NT. The elimination of NT (fewer than 1 case per 1,000 live births) is considered a proxy for maternal tetanus elimination. 2. Surveillance Objectives: The primary goal of NT surveillance is to detect cases to maintain elimination status. This involves ensuring fewer than one NT case per 1,000 live births annually in every district. Secondary objectives include identifying high-risk areas, guiding public health responses, monitoring intervention impacts, and identifying weaknesses in the health system. 3. Surveillance Standards: Nationwide, case-based surveillance is recommended. Every suspected case should be investigated and classified as confirmed or discarded. NT surveillance is population-based, covering all neonates aged 0–28 days. Laboratory confirmation is not required, as diagnosis is clinical. 4. Case Detection and Definition: A suspected NT case is defined as a newborn who could suckle and cry normally during the first two days of life but later lost this ability and developed tetanus-like symptoms or died between 3 and 28 days after birth. Alternatively, any neonatal death of unknown cause within the first month of life is also considered a suspected case. 5. Case Investigation: Suspected cases must be investigated within seven days of notification. The investigation should determine the cause of NT, such as lack of maternal vaccination, unskilled birth attendance, or unhygienic practices. A case investigation form must be completed for every suspected case, documenting findings and actions taken. Feedback should be provided to the reporting facility and community. 6. Unique Case Identification: Each suspected case should be assigned a unique identification number (UID) that includes geographical location, year, and serial number. This UID should be used in all related communications and forms. 7. Protection at Birth (PAB): Protection against NT is assessed based on maternal immunization records and history. A birth is considered protected if the mother received: Two doses of tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (TTCV) during the last pregnancy, with the second dose at least two weeks before delivery. One TTCV dose during the last pregnancy and one or more doses before that pregnancy. No TTCV doses during the last pregnancy but three or more doses at any time before that pregnancy. 8. Differential Diagnosis: Diseases such as meningitis, sepsis (including umbilical sepsis), and birth defects may present with similar symptoms. However, NT is differentiated by the presence of trismus (lockjaw), absence of fontanelle bulging, and spasms triggered by stimuli. 9. Clinical Management: NT is a medical emergency requiring hospitalization. Management includes: Immediate administration of human tetanus immune globulin (TIG) or, if unavailable, equine-derived antitoxin serum (ATS) or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). Muscle spasm control with benzodiazepines. Antibiotics such as metronidazole or penicillin G. Supportive care, including a dark, quiet environment, nasogastric feeding, and airway management. 10. Outbreaks and Public Health Response: NT outbreaks are rare but may occur in clusters linked to substandard clinical care. A rapid community assessment should follow any case investigation, starting from the affected household and extending to others in the area. If maternal immunization coverage is below 90%, corrective actions should include immunization campaigns, community engagement, and education on hygienic cord care. 11. Data Management and Reporting: Designated reporting sites should submit case data regularly, even if no cases are detected (zero reporting). Cases should also be reported annually to WHO/UNICEF through the Joint Reporting Form. Each case must have a unique identifier, and data should include case notification, geographical information, and other relevant details. 12. Sustaining Elimination: Sustaining maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination requires ongoing surveillance, immunization efforts, and public health interventions. Special considerations include integrating maternal immunization into routine health services and training birth attendants. This guide emphasizes the importance of maintaining high-quality surveillance and public health measures to prevent neonatal tetanus and sustain its elimination in the WHO South-East Asia Region.
